messages.body_plain:
Havard,
thanks for the speedy reply.

I had in mind
sigma = exp(eta/2)
as in the stochastic volatility model.
It seems like a natural starting point.

However, I am in "research mode" here, and other options might be equally suitable;
I'd also be interested in allowing a "state-space" model for sigma, but I wasn't sure that
would fit so easily into the INLA framework.

A bit more background:
I'm currently fitting a hierarchical model (without covariates or spatial context of any kind)
to independent observations Y1... Yn, under the model
Y_i | mu_i  \sim N(mu_i, V_i)
mu_i \sim N(0, sigma^2_i)
log(sigma_i) | pi \sim discrete( (a_1, ... a_k), (pi_1,...pi_k))
where discrete (a,pi) takes value a_i with probability pi_i, where pi_1+...+pi_k=1.

My main interest is in the values of mu_i.
Given data Y1...Yn, treating a as known, and V_1... V_n as known, I am estimating pi by maximum likelihood
via a simple EM algorithm, and then computing the posterior p(mu_i | Y_i, pi_hat). [ie I'm using "Empirical Bayes"]

I wanted to extend this to allow mu_1... mu_n to be dependent, by allowing
sigma_1...sigma_n to be dependent.
For example, a Markov random field for the sigma_1... sigma_n instead of independent.
I'm also interested in allowing the distribution of sigma_i to depend on covariates.
I like the discrete distribution for sigma, as it is flexible. However,
I am also interested in leveraging existing fitting methods rather than reinventing
the wheel, so I thought a switch to a gaussian random field model for log(sigma)
might be a reasonable starting point if it allows me to leverage things like INLA.

Best,

Matthew

> r = inla(..., control.inla = list(int.strategy = "grid"),

>
> at least for not to many hyperparameters.
>
> you have to extract the relevant components inside 'x', see str(x) and
> str(x[[1]]), and from these samples, you can generate samples of the
> variable of interest.

> note that the posterior.sample() function is experimental, and future

messages.body_plain:
Dear List,

I would like to fit a bivariate spatial model to a large (55,000 records at 10,000 locations) data set. The key thing is that in addition to fitting separate scale parameters for each response variable, I need to be able to fit an additional scale parameter that controls the behaviour of the cross-covariance between the two responses as a function of distance.  Such a model is described in Section 2.2 of Gneiting et al's  "Matérn cross-covariance functions for multivariate random fields". I have yet to use INLA and I was wondering whether anybody could give me an indication whether such a model would be feasible before I set to learning how to use it?

Thank you.

Jarrod

int.strategy="eb"). if possible, we would recommend using

control.inla = list(int.strategy = "grid")

messages.subject: randow walk within locations
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

We have a dataset spanning about 20 years with data from about 1000 locations. Each location is sampled 6 times per year. A randow walk along year per location would be a good thing for this dataset. We sloved this by creating a new vector year2 = location * (nYear + 200) + year. So year2 looks like 1:20 for location 0,  201:220 for location 1, 401:420 for location 2, ... Then we added a f(year2, model = 'rw1') component to the model. Is this OK or is it rubbish? The example below seems to give reasonable results. Though the year2 effects seems to have some positive bias.

Best regards,

Thierry

library(INLA)
library(ggplot2)
set.seed(12345)
nLocation <- 20
nYear <- 20
nMonth <- 6
Intercept <- 3
Season <- 2
sdYear <- 0.1
sdTrend <- 0.05
sdLocation <- 3
rho <- 0.5
burnin <- 50
probMissing <- 0.2

dataset <- expand.grid(year = seq_len(nYear), month = seq_len(nMonth), location = seq_len(nLocation))
dataset$Fixed <- Intercept + Season * cos(pi * (dataset$month - round(mean(dataset$month))) / nMonth)
Random <- matrix(rnorm(nLocation, mean = 0, sd = sdLocation), ncol = nYear + burnin, nrow = nLocation)

Error <- matrix(rnorm((nYear + burnin) * nLocation, mean = 0, sd = sdYear), ncol = nYear + burnin)
for(i in tail(seq_len(nYear + burnin), -1)){
  Random[, i] <- rho * Random[, i - 1] + Error[, i]
}
Random <- Random[, -seq_len(burnin)]
dataset$Random <- apply(dataset[, c("location", "year")], 1, function(x){
  Random[x["location"], x["year"]]
})
dataset$Random <- dataset$Random + rnorm(nLocation, mean = 0, sd = sdTrend)[dataset$location] * dataset$year
dataset$y <- rpois(nrow(dataset), lambda = exp(dataset$Fixed + dataset$Random))
dataset$y0 <- dataset$y
dataset$y[rbinom(nrow(dataset), prob = probMissing, size = 1) == 1] <- NA
ggplot(subset(dataset, !is.na <http://is.na>(y)), aes(x = year, y = location)) + geom_point() + facet_wrap(~month)
ggplot(dataset, aes(x = year, y = y0, colour = factor(month))) + geom_line() + facet_wrap(~location, scales = "free_y")

dataset$year2 <- with(dataset, location * (nYear + 200) + year)
link <- rep(NA, nrow(dataset))
link[is.na <http://is.na>(dataset$y)] <- 1
model3 <- inla(y ~ factor(month) + f(year2, model = "rw1"), family = "poisson", data = dataset, control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE, link = link))
plot(model3)
test <- merge(dataset, model3$summary.random$year2, by.x = "year2", by.y = "ID")
colnames(test)[11:13] <- c("LCL", "Median", "UCL")
ggplot(test, aes(x = year, y = Random)) + geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = LCL, ymax = UCL), alpha = 0.1, fill = "blue") + geom_line(aes(y = mean), colour = "blue") + geom_line() + facet_wrap(~location, scales = "free_y")

On 08/03/13 10:14, Finn Lindgren wrote:
> Though the year2 effects seems to have some positive bias.

Bear in mind that the rw1 model by default has a sum-to-zero constraint,
which I suspect will make your method behave strangely, partly because
you're not attaching any data to most of the values in the model.  The
"replicate" method would instead applies the sum-to-zero constraint on
each replication, and only has the 20 years for each location, giving
you a lot more control over the model, if for example you want to
include another part of the full model to model the mean values at each
location.

Finn

messages.body_plain:
Dear IOSU,

I have an example with one numeric
covariate and one categorical.
I simulate the data considering a count
response, from zeroinflatedpoisson1 model.
Also, I choose the regression coefficients
with certain values to get some high counts.

###
### simulation process
n <- 1000
altitude <- round(runif(n, 100, 1000))
habitat <- sample(letters[1:5], n, rep=TRUE)

### regression coefficients
beta <- c(-3, 0.005, -1:2)
beta
### the last four coefficients means that
### - specie b have coefficient -1
### - specie c have coefficient 0
### - specie d have coefficient 1
### - specie e have coefficient 2
### we want to simulate counts from Poisson
### distribution with log link.
### so, relative to specie a we have
### - specie b has exp(-1) abundancy relative to specie a (less
abundancy)
### - specie c has same abundancy than specie a (exp(0)==1)
### - specie d has exp(1) abundancy relative to specie a (more ab.)
### - specie e has exp(2) abundancy relative to specie a (more ab.)

### design matrix
xx <- model.matrix(~altitude+habitat)
head(xx) ### habitat is coded to dummie variable
colnames(xx)[1] <- 'Intercept'

### simulation of the locations
coords <- cbind(runif(n, 0, 10), runif(n, 0, 10))
### simulation of the random field
### to do it we need the random field parameters
### and a function to do it easy, bu we just
### take some sine and coside on the coordinates
x <- sin(coords[,1])*3 + cos(coords[,2])*3

plot(coords, cex=1+x/6) ### we have some dependency

### simulating the counts
table(y <- rbinom(n, 1, .7)) ## many zeros
stem(y[y>0] <- rpois(sum(y>0), exp(xx%*%beta + x)[y>0])) ## more zeros
table(y>0)
summary(y)

### fitting the model
### mesh
require(INLA)
bord <- matrix(c(0,10,10,0,0,0,10,10),nc=2)
mesh <- inla.mesh.create.helper(, bord, max.ed=c(.5,1))
plot(mesh)

### prepare the data
Amat <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh, loc=coords)
index <- inla.spde.make.index('i', mesh$n)
stk.d <- inla.stack(list(resp=y), A=list(Amat,1), tag='e',
                    effects=list(index, as.data.frame(xx)))
str(inla.stack.data(stk.d))

### define the spde model and the formulae
spde <- inla.spde2.matern(mesh)
form <- resp ~ 0 + Intercept + altitude + habitatb +
  habitatc + habitatd + habitate + f(i, model=spde)
### fit the model using zeroinflatedpoisson0
res0 <- inla(form, family='zeroinflatedpoisson0',
             data=inla.stack.data(stk.d),
             control.compute=list(dic=T,cpo=T),
             control.predict=list(compute=T, A=inla.stack.A(stk.d)))
### fit the model using zeroinflatedpoisson1
res1 <- inla(form, family='zeroinflatedpoisson1',
             data=inla.stack.data(stk.d),
             control.compute=list(dic=T,cpo=T),
             control.predict=list(compute=T, A=inla.stack.A(stk.d)))
### look at DIC to compare both models
res0$dic$dic
res1$dic$dic ### the best because the data is simulated from this model

res1$summary.fix
res1$summary.hy[1,]

On 18 March 2013 14:13, Lennon <lenno...@gmail.com> wrote:
> My question is what does alpha mean? In 2d space, alpha = nu-1, if I specify
> alpha = 1 then it is modelling matern nu=0?

alpha is the, possibly fractional, order of the differential operator
in the SPDE.
For Matérn models, the corresponding smoothness parameter nu is
alpha-dimension/2.
As you write, dim=2, alpha=1 gives nu=0, which isn't strictly a valid
Matérn model, since it gives a generalised covariance function.  In
that case, the SPDE generates a process which only has meaning as a
random measure, and cannot strictly be interpreted in individual
locations.  The discretised version is however still interpretable
with great care; for a regular lattice it gives a first order
conditional autoregression model, which has been quite popular as a
simple smoothing model.

> and how do we model matern with
> roughness 2?

For dim=2, that corresponds to alpha=3.  The SPDE/GMRF JRSSB Lindgren
et al 2011 paper (see "papers" on r-inla.org <http://r-inla.org>) details what the
precision matrix for that case is, but it is not currently available
as a model in r-inla.

However, if your model lives on a regular lattice however, the
"matern2d" model should allow you to construct such a model.

Finn

Hi,

while the paper happens to use a mesh such that all observation points
are nodes in the mesh, the code in the paper does not actually depend on
that, but instead uses the more general idea that each row of the B
matrix (A.est in the code in the paper) contains interpolation weights
within a triangle.  For the mesh in the paper those weights happen to be
just zeros and a single "1".
Thus you should be able to simply follow the same code as in the paper.

...and now, having looked at what inla.mesh.map.lim() does, the
explanation is simple:
It makes no attempt whatsoever to find a small covering rectangle for
spherical meshes, but _always_ gives the whole globe.
Therefore you'll need to specify the projection limits explicitly.

The reason it does not attempt to do anything more clever is to avoid
surprises for meshes crossing the -180/180 degree longitude line.  For
nice and small convex domains it would be possible, but defining a
sensible method that covers all non-convex and non-connected domains is
hard.  The users themselves however will have a much better idea of what
their domain means and where it is located.
